name: Three Federal Laws in Plain English
title: Three Federal Laws in Plain English
answer: Three federal laws carry most of the protection students have online: FERPA covers education records, COPPA covers the personal information of children under 13 on commercial websites and apps, and CIPA sets filtering and safety rules for schools that receive federal internet discounts. A fourth law, the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment, gives parents rights over surveys and marketing that involve their children. Knowing which law applies matters because AI tools change what each one asks of a school.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The book gathers the main federal student privacy protections into a short list so that school staff can tell them apart. FERPA is about student education records. COPPA is about the personal information of children under 13 when they use commercial websites and apps. CIPA is about internet filtering and safety in schools that receive federal discounts for internet service. The problem this solves is confusion, because without a plain description of each law a school cannot tell which obligation a new AI tool triggers, and the book notes that AI changes what each law asks of a school.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not sort these laws by grade band, with one exception: COPPA's protection is tied to children under 13, so that is the only age line it draws. In day to day school work the laws are described as operating in different places, with FERPA reaching education records, COPPA reaching commercial websites and apps used by younger children, and CIPA reaching the filtering and safety arrangements of schools that take federal internet discounts. The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment is described as mattering less for most AI tools, though it can come into play when a tool asks students about sensitive topics. The book sets the four side by side in Figure 3.2 and then gives each a closer look, with attention to how AI shifts what a school has to do.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text supplies no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice and on the book's plain description of the laws rather than on research findings. The only figure named is Figure 3.2, which sets the four laws side by side, and that is a comparison rather than a piece of evidence. Readers should treat the chapter as an account of what the laws cover and how AI changes the demands on a school, not as a summary of measured outcomes.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that these laws are not the whole picture, since it says three of them do most of the work of protecting students online, which leaves room for other rules and for judgment. The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment is described as mattering less for most AI tools, but it can apply when a tool asks students about sensitive topics, so that situation needs a person to notice it. Which law applies to a given tool, and how that tool is used with students, stays a decision for the school and for parents rather than something the tool settles. This page describes practice as the book sets it out and is not legal advice.
